summary: שָׁבַת is to cease: what was going on stops (day and night, the manna, joy), and someone stops from work, as God ceased on the seventh day from all the work he had made (Gen 2:2–3). The hiphil makes something cease, puts it away or lets it be lacking. שַׁבָּת is the ceasing itself, first the seventh day on which Israel ceases from work, which Yahweh gives as a sign between him and them (Exo 31:13), then the Day of Atonement, the land’s seventh year, and a week counted to a ceasing; שַׁבָּתוֹן is a complete ceasing, which names other feast days too. Punic and Arabic share the verb “come to an end, make cease”, and the New Testament takes the noun over into Greek as σάββατον, for the day and for the week.

words.summary: A ceasing or sitting idle, in three verses. cognates.gloss: cut off, interrupt, put a stop to; rest, cease from work, be still
cognates.note: Arabic s answers to Hebrew ש where Ugaritic and Arabic have š, not ṯ (Arabic ث). Lane’s sources give the transitive verb as “cut off, put a stop to, make cease”, and form VII as “be cut off, cease”; for the sense “rested” they report Azharī’s word that it is not known in the Arabs’ own speech, and the day name السَّبْت is explained from the Jews’ ceasing on it, so those may come from the Sabbath. The verbal noun سُبَات is rest and sleep.

cognates.gloss: the fifteenth day of the month
cognates.note: A day of the lunar month, not the seventh day and not a word for ceasing. Whether the Hebrew noun was borrowed from it, or it from Hebrew, or the two are unrelated, is argued; the Hebrew noun’s meaning follows its own verb “cease”, which Punic and Arabic share, so it is not named on any word.

doctrine.statement: God finished his work and ceased on the seventh day from all of it, and blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because in it he ceased (Gen 2:2–3). Israel is first told of the שַׁבָּת with the manna, before Sinai: none fell on the seventh day, and the people ceased (Exo 16:23–30). The commandment grounds Israel’s ceasing in Yahweh’s own (Exo 20:8–11), and in Deuteronomy in their slavery in Egypt, so that servant and sojourner rest as their master does (Deu 5:12–15). Yahweh calls it a sign between him and Israel, “that you may know that I am Yahweh who makes you holy”, and an everlasting covenant (Exo 31:13–17; Ezk 20:12, 20). In Lev 23 it heads the appointed times of Yahweh (Lev 23:2–3). The prophets set it before foreigners and eunuchs who hold fast to the covenant, whom Yahweh will bring to his holy mountain, for his house is to be called a house of prayer for all peoples (Isa 56:2–7), which Jesus quotes in the temple (Mrk 11:17); and they call it a delight, not doing one’s own ways on it (Isa 58:13–14). Jesus kept the day in the synagogue as his custom was (Luk 4:16), and answered those who accused him: the שַׁבָּת was made for man, not man for the שַׁבָּת, and the Son of Man is lord of it (Mrk 2:27–28); it is lawful to do good on it (Mat 12:12); and a daughter of Abraham bound eighteen years ought to be loosed on the day of the שַׁבָּת (Luk 13:15–16). From the verses: the day rests on what God did, in creating and in bringing out of slavery, and Jesus treats it as given for man’s good and as his own to rule.

Psalm 95 ends with Yahweh’s oath that the generation which hardened its heart would not enter his rest (Psa 95:11). Hebrews reads that rest together with Gen 2:2: God’s works were finished from the foundation of the world, for it is written that God ceased on the seventh day from all his works (Heb 4:3–4). Since Joshua did not give them rest, and David still says “today” long after, “there remains a σαββατισμός”, a keeping of a ceasing, “for the people of God”; the Peshitta has the verb here, “it remains for the people of God to keep a ceasing” (Heb 4:8–9). The one who has entered God’s rest has himself ceased from his works, as God did from his, and so the reader is urged to strive to enter that rest (Heb 4:10–11). From the verses: the ceasing of Gen 2:2 is the pattern of a rest God holds open, which his people enter by ceasing from their own works and do not enter by unbelief.

Yahweh says through the prophets that he cannot bear שַׁבָּת and assemblies kept together with iniquity (Isa 1:13), and that he will make Israel’s feasts, new moons and שַׁבָּתוֹת cease (Hos 2:13). Paul tells the Colossians to let no one judge them in food or drink, or in respect of a feast, a new moon or σάββατα, “which are a shadow of the things to come, but the body is of Christ” (Col 2:16–17). Isaiah, of the new heavens and the new earth, says that from new moon to new moon and from שַׁבָּת to שַׁבָּת all flesh will come to worship before Yahweh (Isa 66:22–23). From the verses: Paul places the שַׁבָּת with the feasts and new moons as a shadow cast by what was to come, whose substance belongs to Christ, and no one is to sit in judgment over another by them; the prophets look to the day being kept by all flesh before Yahweh.

When Israel comes into the land Yahweh gives, the land itself is to cease, a שַׁבָּת to Yahweh: in the seventh year it is not sown or pruned, and what grows of itself is food for the owner, his servants, the hired man, the sojourner and the beasts (Lev 25:2–7). Seven שַׁבְּתֹת of years are counted to the year of jubilee, when liberty is proclaimed and each returns to his possession, for the land is Yahweh’s and Israel are sojourners with him (Lev 25:8–10, 23). If Israel will not keep it, Yahweh will scatter them, and the land will enjoy its שַׁבָּתוֹת while it lies desolate (Lev 26:33–35, 43). Chronicles records it fulfilled: the land enjoyed its sabbaths for seventy years, to fulfil Yahweh’s word by Jeremiah (2Ch 36:21; Jer 25:11). From the verses: the ceasing reaches past people to the land and its creatures, and rests on the land being Yahweh’s, not Israel’s.

note: BDB keys v.az.aa (verb) and v.az.ad (its denominative “keep sabbath”) list the same 71 tokens; v.az.aa is used for the one verb, whose “keep a ceasing” sense (Lev 23:32) is a qal sense. m.dr.bm (מִשְׁבָּת, a cross-reference) has no tokens. Left out: the name שַׁבְּתַי (v.az.af), which belongs in names/; the tokens of יָשַׁב’s infinitive filed here by spelling (Deu 1:6, 1Sa 7:2, Psa 33:14, 127:2, 133:1, Pro 21:19, 25:24); and Amo 6:3 שֶׁבֶת “seat” and Oba 1:3 שִׁבְתּוֹ “his dwelling”, which OSHB lemmatises as 7675 (from ישב) but which the v.az.ab key still counts under שֶׁבֶת. OSHB gives Exo 21:19, Isa 30:7 and Pro 20:3 as 7674, the noun of this root; Exo 21:19 and Isa 30:7 could be read either way. Cognates checked 2026-11-09: Lane pp. 1287–1288 (root سبت), Krahmalkov p. 454 (Š-B-T I; Š-B-T II “share, divide” KAI 3 is a separate problematic root and not entered), Jastrow שְׁבַת and שַׁבְּתָא, Oracc šapattu, Anderson–Moser SEM001087. Not found: Ugaritic šbt “stop” in Segert or Fisher (Segert’s šbt at 1.12 II 59 is “draw water”, not this). Not consulted: Ge’ez ሰንበት (Dillmann), DULAT, CAD šapattu. Arabic سِبِتّ and Syriac ܫܒܬܐ “dill” are a different, borrowed word (Lane n18648: from Persian) and are not cognates. The Peshitta words (SEDRA lexemes 3113 “rest”, verb, Heb 4:9 only; 3114 “Sabbath”) are keyed in SEDRA under the root ܫܒܬܐ, which is why the brief found no Peshitta cognate root; their verses were found from SEDRA’s BFBS word list. Open questions for review: (1) Which שַׁבָּת is meant in מִמָּחֳרַת הַשַּׁבָּת (Lev 23:11, 15–16) is left to the verses: the entry glosses the phrase literally and does not decide between the weekly Sabbath and the first day of מַצּוֹת. (2) The “week” sense rests on Lev 23:15–16 beside Deu 16:9 and on the New Testament’s use; check that this reading of Lev 23:15 is wanted. (3) Whether Arabic sabata “rest” and Ugaritic šbt should be named given the doubts recorded in their notes. (4) Lev 25:6, the produce of the sabbath year called “the שַׁבָּת of the land”, is kept inside the land sense rather than a separate sense.
